I'm testing whether the template shape gets applied directly or mirrored around lone colored cells - in the first example, placing the template near the lone 2 at (8,7) only matches the output if I horizontally flip it, so I'm trying to figure out what determines that mirroring.

Checking example 4, the mirror pattern seems to hold for both lone 2 placements, with 4s appearing on the opposite side from the original template. But in example 2, the same lone-cell placement doesn't require mirroring at all - the offsets match the original template directly, since the template isn't symmetric.

So mirroring isn't a fixed rule; I need to look at example 3's second template to figure out what actually governs it.

In the third template, the lone 2 at (1,10) does get mirrored, matching flipped offsets from the original 4-pattern. But the third shape with 3 and 8 doesn't get mirrored at all, keeping identical offsets. So the mirroring seems inconsistent across shapes within the same grid, which makes me think it might depend on the lone cell's position relative to the grid edges rather than being an inherent property of the shape itself.

Interesting, offsets match exactly again — so shape 3 isn't mirrored either. That contradicts my mirroring theory entirely.

Now I'm reconsidering: maybe it's not about mirroring at all, but something about the lone cell's position relative to the template that determines orientation — perhaps direction away from the grid edge or toward the template's original location. Let me check ex4 shape 2's second copy near row 11 against this positional idea.

Testing another angle: maybe mirroring makes the arm point toward the grid center rather than the template. Checking example 1, the copy's arm points left toward center column 6; checking example 4's shape2 copy similarly seems to point toward center, which could be the actual rule.

Re-examining example 3's lone 2 at (1,10): the offsets from the template are (0,-1),(1,0),(1,1), and the copy's offsets come out mirrored to (0,+1),(1,-1),(1,0) — but if left unmirrored, it would still fit within the grid, so proximity to the edge doesn't explain the mirroring by itself.

Trying a transpose-style reflection instead of mirroring doesn't match the observed offsets either. Looking across examples: ex1 has one lone cell, ex2 has two unmirrored copies, ex3 has one mirrored and one unmirrored, ex4 has two mirrored plus one unmirrored — so maybe the mirroring depends on whether the copy sits to the right or left of the template, with rightward copies getting mirrored.

But checking ex2's second copy at column 9 (right of the template at column 6), the offsets came out identical to the original rather than mirrored, so that column-based rule doesn't hold either. Maybe the shape itself in ex2 is symmetric, which would make mirroring invisible regardless of the rule.

Checking whether the arm orientation in each copy mirrors so it points back toward its template — testing this against ex1, ex2, and ex3, but the direction seems inconsistent depending on which side the copy sits relative to the original.

Now I'm rechecking ex4 shape2 more carefully, tracking the exact offsets of the surrounding 4s relative to the 2's position to see if the mirroring rule actually holds here or breaks down.

Recalculating shows the copy is mirrored even though it sits to the left of the template, contradicting my earlier hypothesis. I'm now wondering if the rule instead depends on vertical mirroring, or on the shape orienting toward/away from the grid center or edges, but neither explanation fits the observed left-side placement. Maybe it's not reflection at all but rotation, so I'm testing whether the offset set matches a 90-degree rotated version of the original shape.

Maybe the mirroring rule isn't about lone-cell count but something else entirely. Let me test the horizontal-mirror hypothesis against example 2's shape, checking whether the offset differences at specific cells match which copy got flipped.

I try another hypothesis: maybe the mirror direction depends on the displacement vector's dominant axis, reflecting perpendicular to it. Testing ex1's displacement of (5,4) against the observed horizontal mirror doesn't quite line up, so I'm not sure that rule holds either.

Checking against ex2's two copies and ex3's shape produces contradictions—cases with similar dominant-axis displacements sometimes mirror and sometimes don't. I need a different angle altogether, maybe something about preserved adjacency rather than displacement direction.

Testing that idea, ex1 turns out to be a horizontal mirror. Since A is transpose-symmetric, I check whether vertical mirror also matches B, but it doesn't, so horizontal mirror is the unique transformation here. I also try both 90-degree rotations to rule them out as alternatives.

Rotating A 90 degrees clockwise gives exactly B, confirming the transformation for ex1. Now I'm testing this same rot90CW rule on ex4's second shape to see if it holds consistently.

Testing 90CW, 90CCW, and 180 rotations for this shape2 case, none match — B turns out to be a mirror image instead. This suggests the transformation isn't a pure rotation but could depend on which direction the shape needs to "point" relative to something else in the grid, like the template's lone cell.

Checking whether grid boundaries constrain orientation — the unmirrored offsets at (1,10) all fit fine inside the grid, so edge-avoidance isn't the deciding factor either. I'm now considering whether the orientation instead relates to the position of the shape's bulk relative to the template location.

Testing this against ex3, ex1, and ex4: in some cases the bulk points toward the template, in others away, so this hypothesis isn't holding consistently. I should go back and double check I've read the ex4 input grid correctly, since my results are conflicting.

Looking again, the shape near (2,8) with its 4s forms an L-like bracket, while the lone 2 sits at (2,3). The output mirrors that bracket shape onto the left side around the lone 2, suggesting the two shapes may be reflections of each other across some vertical axis through the grid's center.

Testing that against example 3's shape3, though, the copy at (8,1) appears unmirrored rather than reflected — likely because a mirrored version would push it out of the grid's bounds. That suggests the actual rule might just be to place the shape wherever it fits within the grid, defaulting to the unmirrored orientation when possible, which matches example 4's copy1 as well.

Testing "points toward center" versus "away from center" against both copies doesn't hold consistently either — copy1 fits pointing away, but copy2 contradicts it. Since both copies share the same orientation, the center-direction theory seems unlikely to be the actual rule.

I realize I don't actually have the test input in front of me yet, so I should default to a translation-style copy of the shape unless the actual test grid gives me more specific clues to work from once it's provided.
